Every entry here was retrieved and checked against **PubMed** — title, journal,
year, authors and DOI. Nothing on this page is a remembered citation. Where a
free full text exists in PubMed Central it is marked **[free]**, because a
curriculum that costs nothing should send you to papers that cost nothing.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Why this page links rather than hosts

We checked the licence of all 28 papers through PubMed. The result is worth
knowing before anyone proposes bundling PDFs with the course:

| | Papers |
|---|---|
| Open licence (all Creative Commons **NC**, several also **ND**) | **6** |
| All rights reserved, but free to *read* on PubMed Central | **15** |
| All rights reserved, no free full text | **7** |
| Carrying a plain **CC BY** licence | **0** |

**Free to read is not free to redistribute.** Twenty-one of these are readable
at no cost on PubMed Central, and that is a permission to read, not a licence to
copy. Redistributing those PDFs — in this repository, in a course pack, in a
shared folder — would infringe copyright.

Even the six openly licensed ones cannot be folded into this site. This
curriculum is **CC BY-SA 4.0**, and BY-SA is incompatible with both **NC**
(non-commercial) and **ND** (no derivatives). We can cite them, describe their
findings, and quote briefly with attribution. We cannot absorb their text or
adapt their figures.

So: **link, never host.** Read them through the DOI or your institution's
subscription. If a lesson needs a figure, we draw our own from the underlying
data or the equations.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The pharmacometrics literature has an unusual gift: *CPT: Pharmacometrics &
Systems Pharmacology* runs a standing tutorial series, most of it open access
and much of it with runnable code in the supplements. If you read nothing else,
read the tutorials.
:::

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/psp.2014.51) · PMID 25531560 · **[free]** | The shortest honest orientation to what population modelling is for. Read before `S2`. |
| Lesko LJ. **Perspective on model-informed drug development.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2021;10:1127–1129. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12699) · PMID 34404115 · **[free]** | What MIDD means and how it became a regulatory process rather than a slogan. |
| Mehrotra S, Gobburu J. **Communicating to influence drug development and regulatory decisions: a tutorial.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2016;5:163–172. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12073) · PMID 27299706 · **[free]** | The skill that decides whether your analysis changes anything. Pairs with `S0-00` §5. |

## Strand P · Pharmacology

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Kenakin T. **Receptor theory.** *Curr Protoc Pharmacol* 2008;Chapter 1:Unit 1.2. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471141755.ph0102s41) · PMID 22294216 | Classical receptor theory and the operational model, by the person who wrote the textbook. Background for `P-04` and `P-05`. |
| Kenakin T. **Biased agonism.** *F1000 Biol Rep* 2009;1:87. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3410/B1-87) · PMID 20948603 · **[free, CC BY-NC 3.0]** | *Read in full.* Dismantles the receptor-as-switch picture: the minimal unit of control is the agonist–receptor complex, not the receptor, so two agonists can have their relative potencies **reverse** between two readouts. Efficacy is "pluridimensional" — propranolol is an antagonist and inverse agonist at G-protein-mediated effects and an *activator* of ERK. The modelling consequence, now in `P-03`: your choice of biomarker decides which effect you are measuring. |
| Dua P, Hawkins E, van der Graaf PH. **A tutorial on target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) models.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2015;4:324–337. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.41) · PMID 26225261 · **[free, CC BY-NC 4.0]** | *Read in full.* Starts exactly where `P-04` stops — with the Langmuir isotherm and the point at which "drug is in vast excess" fails. Then builds the model ladder: full TMDD, quasi-equilibrium, quasi-steady-state, Michaelis–Menten, and **states the conditions under which each approximation holds**, which is the part you cannot reconstruct yourself. Two corrections it supplies to common belief: TMDD is not a biologics-only phenomenon (Levy's first description was warfarin), and TMDD does not by itself imply nonlinear pharmacokinetics. Berkeley Madonna code in the supplement. |
| Anderson BJ, Holford NHG. **Mechanistic basis of using body size and maturation to predict clearance in humans.** *Drug Metab Pharmacokinet* 2009;24:25–36. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2133/dmpk.24.25) · PMID 19252334 | The argument for allometric scaling and for maturation functions in children. Underpins `S0-02` and `P-12`. |
| Rhodin MM, Anderson BJ, Peters AM, et al. **Human renal function maturation: a quantitative description using weight and postmenstrual age.** *Pediatr Nephrol* 2009;24:67–76. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00467-008-0997-5) · PMID 18846389 | GFR from premature neonate to adult in one model. The worked example of why size alone fails in paediatrics. |

## Strand S0 · Foundations

| | Why |
|---|---|
| Beal SL. **Ways to fit a PK model with some data below the quantification limit.** *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 2001;28:481–504. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1012299115260) · PMID 11768292 | The original M1–M7 paper. `S0-03` tells you to flag BLQ and not impute; this is why. |
| Keizer RJ, Karlsson MO, Hooker A. **Modeling and simulation workbench for NONMEM: tutorial on Pirana, PsN, and Xpose.** *CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol* 2013;2:e50. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/psp.2013.24) · PMID 23836189 · **[free, CC BY-NC-ND 3.0]** | *Read in full.* Nominally a software tutorial; in practice the most quotable source on **which diagnostic to trust when**. Supplies the ~5% ε-shrinkage threshold above which \|IWRES\| vs IPRED stops being informative, the sequencing rule (residual-based diagnostics early, simulation-based late), VPC binning guidance (no more bins than observations per individual), the insistence on uncertainty bands rather than bare percentile lines, and bootstrap sample counts (~100 for means, 1,000+ for tail percentiles). Much of `S0-06` now rests on it. |

The remaining seven have no free full text and need a subscription: Beal on BLQ,
Zhao et al. on PBPK best practice, van der Heijden et al. on paediatric PBPK,
Anderson & Holford on size and maturation, Rhodin et al. on GFR maturation,
Kenakin's *Receptor theory*, and Zhu et al. on the MIDD regulatory perspective.
Routes to those, in order of ease: your institution's subscription; an
interlibrary loan; or emailing the corresponding author, which in this field is
normal and usually answered within a day.

Keep what you download in `reading/papers/`. That directory is gitignored, so
your personal library sits beside the project and never enters the repository.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Where the line falls, concretely. **Fine:** downloading these to read, annotate,
and cite. **Not fine:** committing the PDFs here, putting them in a shared drive
for a cohort, or bundling them as a course pack. If you later teach from this
material, course readings go through your library's reserves system, which
exists precisely to license that use.
:::

## What the one-line notes rest on

Honest provenance, because it varies by entry.

We attempted to retrieve full texts through the PubMed Central API. **Full text
came back only for the six openly licensed papers.** For the other twenty-two —
including the fifteen that are free to read in a browser — the API returns the
abstract and an empty body, which tracks the licence status exactly: readable on
the PMC website is not the same as available for programmatic retrieval.

So:

| Entry | The note rests on |
|---|---|
| Dua on TMDD, Keizer on the NONMEM workbench, Kenakin on biased agonism | The full text, read |
| The remaining 3 CC-licensed papers | Retrievable, not yet read |
| The other 22 | Title, journal, abstract, and subject knowledge |

Entries in the second group are a starting map, not a substitute for reading the
paper — and several of them are ones the lessons lean on hardest (Beal on BLQ,
Savic & Karlsson on shrinkage, Anderson & Holford on allometry). Those
annotations describe what the papers are *for*, from their abstracts and their
place in the field, not a close reading.

If a note mischaracterises a paper, that is a bug: open an issue and it gets
fixed.

## How to read a tutorial paper

Do not read it like a review. These have supplements with code, and the code is
the point.

1. Read the abstract and skip to the **worked example**.
2. Download the supplement and **run it before understanding it**. Getting the
   authors' output on your machine is worth more than a careful first read.
3. **Break it** — change a parameter, remove a term, see what the diagnostics do.
   This is `S0-01`'s failure-mode habit applied to somebody else's model.
4. Only then read the theory, with a concrete thing in front of you.

## What is missing here

Honest gaps in this list, which will fill as the strands are written:

- **No textbooks.** Rowland & Tozer, Gabrielsson & Weiner and Rang & Dale are
  each worth owning; none is on PubMed, so none is on this page.
- **No regulatory guidances.** The FDA and EMA population PK, exposure–response
  and PBPK guidances are short, free and tell you exactly what a deliverable
  looks like. They belong in a separate list.
- **Thin on pharmacology proper.** Strand `P` needs primers on ADME, transporters
  and physiology that this first pass did not cover.
- **Nothing on cell and gene therapy kinetics**, which `CASE-CELL` will need.
